interpretations.rationale: Current state: the matrix matches the predicates for twelve of thirteen cases, and one case raises a candidate defect that needs a cleaner witness. Receipt 45b8677c742f492eae4abef8c1cc647b passed and recorded: add-node-a accepted (index 0), add-node-a-again rejected (1), add-observer-b accepted (2), promote-b-same-addr accepted (3), add-observer-c-dup-addr rejected (4), add-witness-w accepted (5), witness-as-observer rejected (6), witness-as-node rejected (7), remove-a accepted (8), readd-removed-a rejected (9), remove-b rejected (10), remove-w accepted (11), remove-only-node accepted (12). The rejections line up with the predicates: duplicate member, duplicate address, witness role changes, re-adding a recorded removed identity, and removing the sole remaining address (remove-b was rejected because node 3 was then the only address). The last event is the concern: node 1 was not in the address set at that point, yet the removal was accepted, and apply() records Removed for the target id while isAddRemovedNode refuses later adds of that id (membership.go:113-120, 208-231, 232-300). The request path performs no membership check for deletions (node.requestConfigChange only validates the target for non-removal types), and the documented contract says a deleted node cannot be added back, which frames removal as deleting a node that is in the cluster (nodehost.go:1132-1151). If a removal of a non-member is accepted, an operator mistake would permanently burn that node identity while nothing is removed. However, the witness used a membership object that never contained the local node, which is not a realistic configuration, so validity of the behavioural claim is not settled. The account stays unresolved with defect_claim unresolved pending the successor probe in a realistic two-node configuration.
counterevidence: Accepting a removal of an unknown identity can be defended as idempotent removal: the post-state has no such member either way, and the only cost is the recorded Removed entry.

The matrix's last case used a membership object without the local node, so it is not a realistic configuration; the same acceptance must be shown from a valid configuration before it can be called a defect.
limitations: Single object-level execution; no raft, node or client API involvement.
The decisive case needs a realistic configuration and a non-member target.
Does not evaluate whether the permanent ban is intended for all removals, only that the documented framing refers to a node deleted from the cluster.
